item.text:
## Research scope and identity

Félix-Antoine Tshisekedi Tshilombo was president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo throughout 2022. The relevant period is 1 January–31 December 2022.

Tshisekedi had formal national authority over security policy, senior military and police appointments, the intelligence services, the justice and prison ministries, and the continuation of the state of siege in North Kivu and Ituri. His attribution is especially strong for the state-of-siege framework and military governors, moderate for recurring national-security-service practices and institutional neglect, and weaker for individual battlefield abuses or decentralized police conduct absent evidence of presidential direction, notice, or obstruction of remedy.

The inherited baseline was exceptionally adverse: longstanding armed conflict, approximately 120 active armed groups in the east, weak civilian control, underfunded justice and detention systems, widespread impunity, and millions already displaced. Reporting remained substantial but incomplete because conflict zones, ANR and military-intelligence detention sites, and some Republican Guard facilities were difficult or impossible for monitors to access.

No score is assigned below.

## Fully extracted evidence

### WEB-3B-001 — State-of-siege powers enabled repression without delivering protection

Tshisekedi’s May 2021 decree transferred civilian authority in North Kivu and Ituri to military and police officers. It allowed unusually broad restrictions on movement, meetings, publications, and public order and routed civilian criminal cases into military courts. Throughout 2022, the government and parliament repeatedly extended the measure without a clear termination test.

Human Rights Watch documented more than two dozen arbitrary arrests, beatings, intimidation incidents, and abusive prosecutions under the regime. Military and police authorities detained legislators, journalists, and activists who criticized its legality or effectiveness. Military courts accumulated backlogs and prolonged pretrial detention. Amnesty counted roughly 30 extensions by September 2022 and described the appointed military and police authorities as accountable to the president.

The protection rationale was not realized. Amnesty compared 559 conflict-related civilian deaths in North Kivu and Ituri during June 2020–March 2021 with at least 1,261 during June 2021–March 2022. This comparison does not prove the state of siege caused the increase—the east faced autonomous armed groups and renewed regional intervention—but it strongly contradicts claims that the exceptional regime had made residents safer.

The ruler connection is high: Tshisekedi decreed the regime, appointed the replacement authorities, publicly tied its end to security conditions, and retained the capacity to seek its termination or narrow its powers. Parliamentary approval of extensions and the operational autonomy of military governors are limiting factors, not breaks in attribution. [Human Rights Watch](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/03/22/dr-congo-martial-law-brings-crackdown-east), [Amnesty International](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/05/drc-one-year-on-state-of-siege/), [Amnesty, September follow-up](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/09/drc-stop-using-prolonged-state-of-siege-as-excuse-to-crush-protests/)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.6, 3B.8, 3B.9, 3B.10.

### WEB-3B-002 — Lethal and threatening treatment of peaceful critics

On 24 January 2022, police dispersing a protest against the state of siege in Beni shot 22-year-old LUCHA activist Mumbere Ushindi in the abdomen; he died shortly afterward. Before the demonstration, the local police commander threatened protesters with disappearance from their families. After the shooting, the police officer serving as mayor referred to protesters as dogs and said authorities arrested and killed them. Police then detained 12 activists traveling to Ushindi’s funeral for two nights.

This is unusually strong evidence of a physical-safety violation linked to official repression: the victim was a peaceful critic, police used lethal force, and senior local security officials publicly voiced violent and dehumanizing threats. It does not establish that Tshisekedi ordered or personally endorsed the rhetoric or killing. Presidential attribution instead arises through the state-of-siege command structure and the lack of an identified prompt, independent investigation or remedy after prominent public reporting.

In April 2022, police also used excessive force against an opposition sit-in at parliament in Kinshasa, injuring at least 20 people. In September, security forces injured several participants while breaking up a peaceful medical-union demonstration. These incidents indicate a broader protest-policing problem, but the available sources do not document presidential orders and therefore support only moderate ruler attribution. [Human Rights Watch, March investigation](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/03/22/dr-congo-martial-law-brings-crackdown-east), [Human Rights Watch, events of 2022](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.3, 3B.6, 3B.8, 3B.9.

### WEB-3B-003 — Torture by state agents remained widespread and remedies were weak

A joint OHCHR–MONUSCO study covering April 2019–April 2022 documented 1,293 acts by state agents affecting 2,295 victims. FARDC personnel accounted for 746 violations and 1,399 victims; police for 453 violations and 750 victims; the ANR for 47 violations and 65 victims. Approximately 93 percent of documented cases occurred in conflict-affected provinces. The report connected torture to detention, conflict operations, and restrictions on democratic space.

The report found that the pre-existing 2011 anti-torture law and the National Human Rights Commission supplied a formal legal framework, but implementation was deficient. The commission rarely used its detention-inspection and investigation powers, partly because of inadequate resources. The newly created national torture-prevention committee lacked clearly secured resources, institutional independence, operational autonomy, and an effective oversight mechanism.

Across the full study period, authorities obtained convictions of two FARDC soldiers, 12 police officers, one ANR agent, and 75 armed-group members for torture or cruel treatment. None of the listed convictions occurred in January–April 2022. Reparations remained rare. UN monitors did secure some releases through weekly engagement with the ANR and military intelligence, but those services continually denied monitors physical access to their detention sites.

The period spans much of Tshisekedi’s presidency but is not a 2022-only statistic. It establishes a recurring structure inherited from earlier administrations that remained materially unreformed into 2022. It does not establish that Tshisekedi personally directed torture. It does establish notice, formal authority, weak preventive mechanisms, low accountability relative to documented abuse, and continuing secrecy around nationally controlled intelligence detention. [OHCHR–MONUSCO joint report, pp. 8, 17, 27–30](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/torture/2022-10-04/041022_Joint-report-on-torture-in-the-DRC-01042019-to-30042022.pdf)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.7.

### WEB-3B-004 — Arbitrary and incommunicado detention remained routine

The 2022 U.S. human-rights report found that security officials routinely violated warrant, 48-hour presentation, notice, family-contact, and counsel requirements. Protesters and civil-society activists were regularly held incommunicado and without charge. The ANR, military intelligence, and Republican Guard operated unofficial or inaccessible detention sites and sometimes refused to acknowledge detentions.

Illustrative 2022 cases included former presidential security adviser François Beya, arrested by the ANR in February and held for four months before formal charges, and former ruling-party leader Jean-Marc Kabund, arrested after breaking with Tshisekedi and charged in part with contempt of the head of state. Beya received provisional release on health grounds in August. These politically salient cases raise concern about selective security-law enforcement, though neither source conclusively establishes that the accusations were fabricated or that Tshisekedi personally ordered the arrests.

A favorable institutional fact is that courts sometimes ordered releases: after ANR agents stripped and beat three journalists in Boende in May, a High Court judge ordered their unconditional release the following day. That remedy did not itself establish accountability for the alleged torture. [U.S. Department of State report hosted by ecoi, §§1.c–1.d](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html), [Human Rights Watch, events of 2022](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.5, 3B.8.

### WEB-3B-005 — Life-threatening prison conditions and obstructed monitoring

UNJHRO recorded 133 deaths in detention during the first half of 2022, mostly associated with malnutrition, poor hygiene, lack of medical care, and mistreatment. National prison occupancy was estimated at approximately 200 percent, with some institutions exceeding 500 percent. Makala prison, built for 1,500 people, held as many as 9,652.

Food, medicine, sanitation, staffing, and recordkeeping were grossly inadequate. Women were sometimes imprisoned with their children, juveniles were held with adults, and some child survivors of sexual violence were detained alongside adults. Authorities often prevented complaints to judicial bodies and rarely investigated credible mistreatment allegations. The government generally allowed the ICRC, MONUSCO, and NGOs into ordinary Justice Ministry facilities, but sometimes denied access to Republican Guard, ANR, and military-intelligence sites.

The source also records limited mitigation: some people detained on minor charges were released to reduce congestion. Yet the scale of deaths and overcrowding indicates that these releases did not provide an effective remedy. Because the Justice Ministry controlled ordinary prisons and national security agencies controlled the closed sites, ruler-level attribution is moderate through funding, appointments, and feasible institutional action. It is weaker for individual provincial-prison decisions. [U.S. Department of State report hosted by ecoi, §§1.c–1.d](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.7.

### WEB-3B-006 — Some accountability occurred, but impunity remained the dominant pattern

UNJHRO reported that during the first half of 2022, courts convicted 41 FARDC soldiers, 12 police officers, and 102 armed-group members for conduct constituting human-rights abuses. A later UNJHRO annual summary, reported by Actualité.cd, gave full-year totals of 71 soldiers and 20 police officers convicted for offenses connected to human-rights violations. These proceedings are meaningful contrary evidence against a claim of complete official impunity.

Their significance is nevertheless limited. The public summaries do not show the share of reported violations investigated, the seniority of those convicted, whether commanders or politically protected actors were reached, whether judgments became final, or whether victims received reparations. UN reporting also noted continued appointments of officers facing serious abuse allegations. The joint torture report found no listed torture convictions during January–April 2022 and described reparations as rare.

Tshisekedi can reasonably receive some attribution for permitting courts and UN-supported accountability mechanisms to operate, but the records do not establish that he personally initiated the cases. Conversely, raw conviction counts alone cannot demonstrate an effective national remedy. [U.S. Department of State report](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html), [Actualité.cd summary of UNJHRO annual findings](https://actualite.cd/index.php/2023/02/08/rdc-durant-lannee-2022-71-militaires-et-20-policiers-ont-ete-condamnes-pour-des), [OHCHR–MONUSCO torture report](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/torture/2022-10-04/041022_Joint-report-on-torture-in-the-DRC-01042019-to-30042022.pdf)

Lenses: 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.9.

### WEB-3B-007 — Government forces abused children and survivors of sexual violence, alongside genuine preventive steps

For January–June 2022, UNJHRO documented 239 conflict-related sexual-violence cases affecting women and children; nearly 18 percent were attributed to state agents. FARDC personnel were linked to 54 survivors, including 24 children. The Congolese report also found security-force abuse of street-connected children and persistent failure to enforce laws against domestic violence, forced marriage, and child abuse.

A UN Secretary-General report covering April 2020–March 2022 found 233 children detained for alleged armed-group association—216 by FARDC, 15 by police, and two by the ANR—despite directives requiring their transfer to child-protection organizations. During the reporting window, 143 children killed or maimed and 256 instances of sexual violence against children were attributed to government forces. Those cumulative figures cannot be treated as 2022-only outcomes, but the report separately identified continued violations in the first quarter of 2022.

There was material favorable evidence. FARDC and police issued action plans against conflict-related sexual violence in January 2022, began monthly implementation meetings with UNJHRO in May, received command-level training, maintained specialized child-protection and sexual-violence police capacity, and continued screening intended to prevent child recruitment. Armed groups, not state forces, committed the large majority of verified child abductions and conflict abuses. These measures demonstrate policy effort, although they had not eliminated operational abuse and implementation remained uneven. [U.S. Department of State report, §§1.g and 6](https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html), [UN Secretary-General, S/2022/745, pp. 7–9](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3994129/files/S_2022_745-EN.pdf)

Lenses: 3B.1, 3B.2, 3B.4, 3B.7, 3B.9.

### WEB-3B-008 — Civilian insecurity worsened despite security operations

Human Rights Watch reported that armed actors killed at least 2,446 civilians in South Kivu, North Kivu, and Ituri from January through late October 2022. At least 155 deaths were attributed to Congolese security forces. Armed groups and government forces together killed more than 2,000 people in the two state-of-siege provinces. Nearly 5.6 million people were internally displaced nationally by July.

UCDP identified the DRC as the world’s third most conflict-affected country in the first half of 2022. In June alone, the DRC experienced more than 300 civilian deaths from deliberate one-sided violence. UCDP’s public summary indicates that Islamic State-linked actors contributed heavily to this toll; it does not attribute the June aggregate to the Congolese government.

The revived M23 offensive, Rwandan support to M23, ADF and CODECO atrocities, intercommunal violence, and the state’s limited reach sharply constrain personal attribution to Tshisekedi. Nevertheless, the continued state of siege, ineffective joint operations against ADF, and failure to process thousands of surrendered fighters through demobilization were within the national government’s policy domain. HRW reported that many surrendered combatants returned to armed groups.

The government did pursue responses: it conducted or joined military operations, deployed forces during the Teke–Yaka crisis, participated in Nairobi talks, joined the East African Community, and supported regional-force deployment. These actions show an attempt to protect civilians but did not produce improved safety during 2022. [Human Rights Watch, events of 2022](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo), [UCDP 2022 organized-violence summary](https://ucdp.uu.se/downloads/newsletter/issue5.html)

Lenses: 3B.2, 3B.6, 3B.7, 3B.9, 3B.10.

### WEB-3B-009 — FARDC cooperation with abusive armed groups weakened civilian protection

During the M23 resurgence, Congolese forces cooperated with a coalition of local armed groups. One participant was Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, an NDC-R faction leader wanted by Congolese authorities for serious crimes including rape and child recruitment. UN Group of Experts reporting also documented FARDC cooperation with armed groups while separately establishing Rwandan support to M23 and serious M23 abuses.

This evidence does not show that Tshisekedi personally selected Guidon or ordered particular abuses. It does establish a national-force nexus to actors accused of grave crimes and raises questions about vetting, command control, and tolerance under military pressure. The M23 offensive and foreign intervention are substantial limiting circumstances; they explain the security incentive for local alliances but do not remove the government’s duty to protect civilians or prevent abusive auxiliaries from operating with official forces. [Human Rights Watch, events of 2022](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo), [Congo Research Group summary of UN Group of Experts findings](https://www.congoresearchgroup.org/en/2022/11/09/goe-report-why-knowing-the-facts-isnt-enough/)

Lenses: 3B.2, 3B.6, 3B.7, 3B.9.

### WEB-3B-010 — Year-end victim-protection and reparations law

On 26 December 2022, Tshisekedi promulgated Law No. 22/065 concerning protection and reparations for victims of conflict-related sexual violence and crimes against peace and human security. It recognized rights to truth, justice, reparation, guarantees of non-repetition, humanitarian assistance, family reunification, participation in policy, and safe and dignified return.

This was a significant favorable institutional measure within direct presidential authority. It supplied a potential legal basis for remedies to victims who previously faced rare compensation and fragmented assistance. Because it took effect at the very end of the period, it cannot establish that reparations were actually delivered during 2022. Later implementation, funding, institutional independence, accessibility outside major cities, and treatment of abuses committed by state agents require separate verification. [Text of Law No. 22/065](https://www.leganet.cd/Legislation/Droit%20Public/DH/Loi.022.65.26.12.2022.html)

Lenses: 3B.4, 3B.7, 3B.9.

## Cross-lens synthesis

The strongest ruler-specific evidence concerns Tshisekedi’s continuation of the state of siege. It was a presidentially initiated emergency framework, retained through 2022 despite documented repression, military-court dysfunction, repeated criticism, and worsening civilian casualties. This connects directly to due process, emergency powers, protest treatment, crisis response, and end-period safety.

State abuses were recurrent rather than isolated: torture, arbitrary and incommunicado detention, lethal or excessive protest policing, prison deaths, sexual violence, and child detention appeared across independent UN, NGO, and diplomatic reporting. Evidence does not establish a personal presidential order for these abuses or a nationally systematic exterminatory policy. Attribution more often rests on command structure, institutional continuity, notice, appointments, continued emergency policy, and insufficient remedy.

Contrary evidence is real and should be preserved. Courts convicted some soldiers, police, and armed-group members; judges ordered some detainees released; monitors obtained releases through engagement with intelligence services; FARDC and police adopted action plans and training against sexual violence and child recruitment; and Tshisekedi promulgated a victim-protection and reparations law. These measures were too limited, too late, or too weakly implemented to erase the underlying evidence, but they prevent describing 2022 as a year of total institutional inaction.

No inspected source identified Tshisekedi personally inciting ethnic hatred or calling for violence against opponents during 2022. The clearest dehumanizing rhetoric came from state-of-siege police officials in Beni. Attribution to the president is institutional and remedial, not personal-incitement attribution.

## Opened corroboration

- The U.S. Department of State report was opened through ecoi, which reproduces the report and provides stable paragraph-level text. It is comprehensive but often relies on UN and NGO findings, creating duplication risk.
- The OHCHR–MONUSCO torture report was inspected directly as a primary UN PDF. Its aggregate reporting window is April 2019–April 2022, requiring careful period labeling.
- The UN Secretary-General’s children-and-armed-conflict report was inspected directly. Its reporting period is April 2020–March 2022, and cumulative figures must not be represented as 2022 totals.
- HRW’s March investigation and 2023 World Report chapter were inspected directly. The former provides detailed named cases; the latter is an annual synthesis and partly relies on Kivu Security Tracker, UN, and press data.
- Amnesty’s May and September 2022 state-of-siege reports were inspected directly. The May briefing was based on 44 interviews and document review.
- UCDP’s public 2022 newsletter was inspected directly. It establishes conflict intensity and one-sided violence but does not supply a ruler-specific DRC perpetrator table.
- The text of Law No. 22/065 was located through Leganet. It is a legal-text repository rather than the official gazette; the law’s existence is independently corroborated by later UN reporting.

## Uninspected or incompletely inspected leads

- The underlying UNJHRO 2022 annual statistical report behind the MONUSCO and Actualité.cd summaries should be obtained locally or from a UN archive. It may provide disaggregated perpetrator, province, victim, and accountability totals.
- The UCDP GED and One-sided Violence datasets should be queried locally for DRC 2021–2022 actor-year records. The newsletter does not distinguish every perpetrator or furnish a complete annual total.
- CIRIGHTS, PTS, and V-Dem 2022 local records were unavailable in this browsing environment. They should be added as structured country-year context, not treated as ruler-specific proof.
- The July 2022 anti-MONUSCO protests merit a dedicated incident reconstruction. Available reporting indicates 32 demonstrators or bystanders and four peacekeepers died, but the inspected Amnesty source did not disaggregate which civilian deaths were caused by Congolese forces, UN personnel, or other violence.
- Presidential and parliamentary records should be collected for every 2022 state-of-siege extension, including any proposed safeguards, reviews, or objections.
- Follow-up records are needed on investigations into Mumbere Ushindi’s killing, the violent July protests, alleged torture by ANR officers in Boende, and complaints against Goma’s military mayor.
- Implementation records for Law No. 22/065—including funding, claims received, payments, and institutional governance—are predominantly post-period and should be reserved for retrospective analysis.
- A focused French-language search of CNDH, LUCHA, JED, Radio Okapi, Actualité.cd, and parliamentary archives could clarify domestic complaint handling and official responses.

## Rejected or non-evidentiary sources

- Wikipedia pages concerning the anti-MONUSCO protests, individual massacres, or the general DRC conflict were excluded because stronger underlying UN, NGO, legal, or event-data sources were available.
- Reddit reposts and automated summaries were excluded because they were derivative and did not improve provenance.
- Reports about the August 2023 Goma/Wazalendo massacre were excluded from the 2022 evidentiary record. They may be relevant later as retrospective evidence of institutional persistence, but they do not establish a 2022 fact.
- Broad macroeconomic, pandemic, donor-program, and corruption material was excluded unless it established a direct physical-safety connection.
- M23 and foreign-force abuses were not attributed to Tshisekedi merely because they occurred during his presidency. They appear only as inherited/external constraints or where government policy, force cooperation, or protection performance is directly relevant.

## Remaining questions and saturation assessment

The main unresolved issues are:

- whether Tshisekedi or his immediate office received and acted upon specific reports of abuse by military governors;
- whether senior commanders, rather than only rank-and-file personnel, faced accountability;
- the precise 2022 PTS, CIRIGHTS, V-Dem, and UCDP measures;
- investigation outcomes for major protest and detention cases;
- whether any presidential rhetoric materially encouraged hostility or violence;
- national, exposure-adjusted trends outside the heavily reported eastern provinces; and
- whether the December reparations law subsequently delivered effective remedies.

Additional broad web searching is now likely to repeat the established patterns. Material gains are most likely from the local structured datasets, the complete UNJHRO annual report, official state-of-siege extension records, and case-specific judicial files.

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Democratic Republic of the Congo","publisher":"U.S. Department of State","publication_date":"2023-03-20","url":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html","claim":"UNJHRO recorded 133 detention deaths in the first half of 2022, while severe overcrowding, hunger, inadequate medical care, corruption, failure to investigate mistreatment, detention of children with adults, and restricted access to security-service facilities created life-threatening conditions.","locator":"Section 1.c, prison and detention center conditions, lines 79-96","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-005","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_life_threatening_detention_conditions","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.7"],"source_type":"government_human_rights_report_using_un_monitoring","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Contains specific UN-derived counts and institutional detail; some national estimates and causal descriptions are secondary.","final_evidence_use":"Shows preventable physical insecurity and deaths within state custody.","period_fit":"requested_period","ruler_attribution":"moderate through Justice Ministry funding, prison administration, and nationally controlled closed sites; weaker for individual provincial management","contrary_evidence":"Authorities released some minor-offense detainees to reduce crowding and generally allowed monitors into ordinary Justice Ministry prisons.","lenses":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.7"]}  
SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Democratic Republic of the Congo","publisher":"U.S. Department of State","publication_date":"2023-03-20","url":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html","claim":"During the first half of 2022, courts convicted 41 FARDC soldiers, 12 police officers, and 102 armed-group members for acts constituting human-rights abuses, demonstrating limited but genuine accountability amid persistent impunity.","locator":"Section 1.c, accountability discussion, lines 72-78","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-006","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_security_force_accountability_convictions","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.4","3B.9"],"source_type":"government_human_rights_report_using_un_monitoring","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Specific UNJHRO-derived figures; public summary lacks denominators, seniority, final-judgment status, and victim-remedy outcomes.","final_evidence_use":"Preserves favorable evidence of prosecutions while calibrating their limited systemic meaning.","period_fit":"requested_period","ruler_attribution":"low_to_moderate; proceedings occurred under Tshisekedi but personal initiation is not established","contrary_evidence":"Convictions were few relative to documented abuse; senior or protected commanders were not shown to have been reached, and reparations remained rare.","lenses":["3B.2","3B.4","3B.9"]}  
SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Children and armed conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: Report of the Secretary-General","publisher":"United Nations Secretary-General","publication_date":"2022-10-10","url":"https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3994129/files/S_2022_745-EN.pdf","claim":"For April 2020-March 2022, the UN verified detention of 233 children for alleged armed-group association, mainly by FARDC, and substantial killing, maiming, sexual violence, and attacks on schools attributable to government forces; violations continued into the first quarter of 2022.","locator":"S/2022/745, pp. 7-9, paras. 32-47","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-007","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_children_harmed_and_detained_by_state_forces","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.7","3B.9"],"source_type":"un_secretary_general_monitoring_report","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Primary UN verification with disaggregation by perpetrator and violation; cumulative reporting period is not a calendar-2022 total.","final_evidence_use":"Establishes serious vulnerable-group exposure to state as well as armed-group violence.","period_fit":"mixed_period_ending_march_2022","ruler_attribution":"moderate for FARDC, police, and ANR policy and compliance; weak for individual incidents without command evidence","contrary_evidence":"Armed groups committed most grave violations; government screening, action plans, training, and UN cooperation represented meaningful preventive efforts.","lenses":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.7","3B.9"]}  
SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"World Report 2023: Democratic Republic of Congo — Events of 2022","publisher":"Human Rights Watch","publication_date":"2023-01-12","url":"https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo","claim":"At least 2,446 civilians were killed by armed actors in three eastern provinces from January to late October 2022, including at least 155 by Congolese security forces; nearly 5.6 million people were displaced and the state of siege did not curb violence.","locator":"Lines 61-87, especially lines 64, 67, and 76-85","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-008","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_civilian_deaths_displacement_and_security_deterioration","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10"],"source_type":"independent_annual_human_rights_synthesis","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Uses Kivu Security Tracker and UN data and distinguishes some perpetrators; eastern geographic concentration and mixed actors limit national and ruler-specific inference.","final_evidence_use":"Establishes worsening end-period physical insecurity while preserving the dominant non-state and external causes.","period_fit":"requested_period","ruler_attribution":"moderate for policy performance and state-force deaths, low for autonomous armed-group and foreign-backed violence","contrary_evidence":"M23's resurgence, Rwandan support, ADF, CODECO, and roughly 120 armed groups severely constrained state capacity; government pursued military, diplomatic, and regional responses.","lenses":["3B.2","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10"]}  
SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"World Report 2023: Democratic Republic of Congo — Events of 2022","publisher":"Human Rights Watch","publication_date":"2023-01-12","url":"https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/democratic-republic-congo","claim":"FARDC fought M23 alongside a coalition containing armed groups, including a faction commanded by wanted militia leader Guidon Shimiray Mwissa, who was implicated in rape and child recruitment.","locator":"Lines 76-86 and 103","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-009","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_fardc_cooperation_with_abusive_armed_groups","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9"],"source_type":"independent_annual_human_rights_synthesis","source_confidence":"medium_high","source_confidence_reason":"Specific actor and alliance identified and consistent with UN Group of Experts reporting; command authorization and the conduct of allied groups during particular operations need fuller reconstruction.","final_evidence_use":"Shows a state nexus to abusive auxiliaries and weaknesses in vetting and command control.","period_fit":"requested_period","ruler_attribution":"moderate for national military alliance policy; no evidence Tshisekedi personally selected Guidon or directed abuse","contrary_evidence":"The coalition formed amid a major foreign-backed M23 offensive; security necessity may explain but does not excuse cooperation with abusive actors.","lenses":["3B.2","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9"]}  
SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON:{"title":"Loi n°22/065 du 26 décembre 2022 fixant les principes fondamentaux relatifs à la protection et à la réparation des victimes","publisher":"Democratic Republic of the Congo, text reproduced by Leganet","publication_date":"2022-12-26","url":"https://www.leganet.cd/Legislation/Droit%20Public/DH/Loi.022.65.26.12.2022.html","claim":"Tshisekedi promulgated a law recognizing rights to truth, justice, reparation, non-repetition, assistance, participation, family reunification, and safe return for victims of conflict-related sexual violence and crimes against peace and human security.","locator":"Statement of purpose and Article 14","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-010","canonical_fact_key":"drc_2022_victim_protection_and_reparations_law","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.4","3B.7","3B.9"],"source_type":"legal_record","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Reproduces the enacted statutory text and is corroborated by UN reporting; Leganet is not itself the official gazette.","final_evidence_use":"Favorable evidence of a ruler-attributable legal remedy created at year end, with implementation untested during the period.","period_fit":"requested_period_year_end","ruler_attribution":"high for promulgation; implementation outcomes not established","contrary_evidence":"The law was enacted five days before year end, so it provides no evidence of 2022 payments, access, enforcement, or institutional effectiveness.","lenses":["3B.4","3B.7","3B.9"]}
